summary: Review holo implementation: spec compliance, correctness, robustness — with adversarial verification

confirmed.title: `holo` does not restore the TUI after quitting it — q → `holo` round-trip leaves a session with no TUI window
confirmed.description: Spec line 215 says `holo` = "attach/start tmux session + TUI", and line 167 says `q` quits the TUI while daemon + sessions keep running. When the TUI process exits (q, or SIGINT), its tmux window 'tui' dies with it. `RealTmux.ensureSession` (tmux.ts:65) only creates the TUI window when the whole session is missing (`if (!(await this.sessionExists()))`), so re-running `holo` while agent windows are still alive attaches to a session with no TUI window. The spec's primary re-entry loop is broken: there is no TUI, `selectTuiWindow` (`select-window -t holo:tui`, index.tsx:98) fails silently, and the spec-mandated `prefix+Space` return binding targets the nonexistent `holo:tui` window, so it does nothing from agent windows. The only recovery is manually creating a window and running `holo tui`, or killing the whole session.
confirmed.suggestion: In `ensureSession` (or the attach path in cli.ts), when the session already exists, check whether a window named 'tui' is present (`list-windows -F '#{window_name}'`) and respawn it with `new-window -n tui <tuiArgv>` if missing, before installing the return binding.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing code. (1) The TUI window is created by `new-session -d -s holo -n tui '<tuiArgv>'` in RealTmux.ensureSession (tui/src/tmux.ts:65-78); the window runs the TUI process directly, no `remain-on-exit` is set anywhere in tui/src, so tmux destroys the window when the process exits. (2) `q` in the TUI (ui/App.tsx:122-123) calls onQuit → `process.exit(0)` (index.tsx:65); SIGINT exits 130 — either way the tui window dies while agent windows keep the session alive. (3) Re-running `holo` hits the attach path (cli.ts:189-199) → ensureSession, whose window creation is guarded by `if (!(await this.sessionExists()))` — with the session alive it only reinstalls the binding, never recreating the tui window. The daemon's spawn path (daemon/server.ts:273) uses the same guarded ensureSession. No code checks for a window named 'tui' or respawns it (grep confirms the only ':tui' refs are selectWindow in index.tsx:98 and the bind target in tmux.ts:131). (4) The failure is silent: defaultRunner resolves non-zero statuses and RealTmux.selectWindow ignores the status, so `select-window -t holo:tui` fails invisibly, and the prefix+Space binding targets a nonexistent window. (5) Not covered by tests — FakeTmux.ensureSession just sets a boolean and doesn't model the tui window — and not in the known-intentional deviations list. Severity 'major' is honest: `holo` (no args → attach, cli.ts:39) is the spec's primary re-entry command (spec CLI section: "attach/start tmux session + TUI"), and the q → holo round trip breaks whenever any agent window survives, which is the normal operating mode; recovery requires manual tmux intervention. Suggested fix (check `list-windows -F '#{window_name}'` for 'tui' and respawn when missing) is sound.

confirmed.title: Real-Claude integration smoke layer is missing
confirmed.description: Spec Testing section (line 240): "Real-Claude integration is a thin smoke layer: spawn interactive `claude` in a headless tmux session (pre-trusted cwd), drive it with `tmux send-keys`, assert daemon state transitions from real hook events… wait on the `SessionStart` hook for readiness rather than sleeping." No such test exists anywhere (grep for send-keys/smoke finds nothing). The only end-to-end test (src/e2e.test.ts) runs FakeAgent against FakeTmux — it never touches a real tmux server or a real harness. This matters doubly because docs/hooks-research.md itself flags that end-to-end firing of codex `-c`-injected hooks is "source-verified but not live-tested", so the entire claude/codex injection path (claude --settings, codex -c overrides, the injected hook command, the PermissionRequest stdout protocol) has zero automated real-world validation.
confirmed.suggestion: Add a skipped-by-default (env-gated, e.g. HOLO_SMOKE=1) integration test that starts the daemon with RealTmux, spawns `claude` via the ClaudeAdapter in a pre-trusted tmp cwd, waits on the SessionStart-driven 'ready' transition, drives a prompt via `tmux send-keys`, and asserts running→idle transitions from real hook events.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading the code. (1) tui/spec.md line 240 explicitly specifies a real-Claude smoke layer: spawn interactive `claude` in headless tmux, drive via `tmux send-keys`, assert daemon transitions from real hook events, wait on SessionStart for readiness. (2) No such test exists anywhere: grep for send-keys/smoke/SMOKE across tui/src, tui/docs, and tui/*.md hits only spec.md; no skipIf/env-gated/skipped tests exist in any of the 15 test files. (3) src/e2e.test.ts is confirmed to use FakeTmux + FakeAdapter + fake-agent child process — real daemon and real Unix socket, but never a real tmux server or real harness binary. tmux.test.ts exercises RealTmux only through an injected fake TmuxRunner (argv capture, never executes tmux). claude/codex/server tests spawn no real binaries. (4) docs/hooks-research.md line 66 confirms the risk amplifier: end-to-end firing of -c-injected codex hooks is 'source-verified but not live-tested — flagged risk', so the claude --settings and codex -c injection paths have zero automated real-world validation. (5) Not covered by any of the 8 known-intentional deviations. Severity 'major' is honest for a spec-compliance review: an entire spec-mandated test layer is missing, and it covers the riskiest integration mechanism the daemon depends on, flagged as untested by the project's own research doc.

confirmed.title: tmux return binding key is hardcoded — spec says configurable
confirmed.description: Spec line 169: "a tmux binding (default `prefix+Space`, configurable) returns to the TUI window". `RealTmux.installReturnBinding` (tmux.ts:125-133) hardcodes `bind-key Space`. There is no env var or config knob to change the key (only HOLO_TMUX_SESSION exists for the session name). The known-deviation list covers the binding being server-global, not its non-configurability — a user whose prefix+Space is already bound (common: next-layout) has no recourse.
confirmed.suggestion: Read the key from an env var (e.g. HOLO_RETURN_KEY, default 'Space') in installReturnBinding, mirroring the HOLO_TMUX_SESSION pattern in paths.ts.

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the code. Spec (tui/spec.md:169) explicitly says the return binding is "(default `prefix+Space`, configurable)" — and unlike jump-on-spawn (line 204, "configurable later"), there is no deferral, nor does the v1 "Out" scope list exclude it. RealTmux.installReturnBinding (tui/src/tmux.ts:125-133) hardcodes the literal 'Space'; the only env knobs in the codebase are HOLO_HOME, HOLO_TMUX_SESSION, and HOLO_FAKE_SCRIPT (paths.ts, adapters/fake.ts) — no key override exists. cli.ts:257 hardcodes the "prefix+Space" message and tmux.test.ts:105/115/201 assert the exact literal, confirming no configuration path. The known-intentional deviation #2 covers only the binding being server-global, a distinct property from key configurability; the tmux.ts doc comment (lines 45-51) likewise documents only the server-global deviation. The failure scenario is concrete: prefix+Space is tmux's default next-layout binding, and ensureSession (tmux.ts:77) re-installs the binding unconditionally on every call, so even a user who rebinds Space in .tmux.conf gets it clobbered again — genuinely no recourse. Severity "minor" is honest for a missing config knob.

confirmed.title: An aged needs_input ties a fresh permission at score 100 and outranks it — "permissions jump the queue" violated at the boundary
confirmed.description: Spec line 125: "Permissions jump the queue — they're 2-second decisions blocking an agent." A needs_input session waiting ≥20 minutes scores 60+40(cap)=100, equal to a fresh permission's 100. buildQueue's tie-break (scoring.ts:40-43) is statusSince ascending, so the older needs_input ranks ABOVE the permission: the queue top is not the blocking permission, and `holo next` jumps to the needs_input item instead. The weights are implemented exactly per the formula, but the chosen tie-break contradicts the normative "permissions jump the queue" sentence in the one case the formula allows a tie.
confirmed.suggestion: Tie-break by status before statusSince (permission first), e.g. insert `statusRank(b) - statusRank(a)` between the score and statusSince comparisons in buildQueue.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the code. (1) The tie is arithmetically reachable: scoring.ts gives needs_input 60+40(cap)=100 at >=20 full minutes, fresh permission 100+0=100. (2) buildQueue (scoring.ts:39-44) tie-breaks by statusSince ascending after score, so the older needs_input ranks above the fresh permission — and the project's own test (scoring.test.ts:134-146, 'breaks cross-status score ties by older statusSince first') constructs this exact permission-vs-aged-needs_input scenario and asserts the needs_input comes first, proving the behavior is concrete and deterministic. (3) The 'next' handler (server.ts:201-211) takes queue[0] and selects its tmux window, so `holo next` does jump to the needs_input instead of the blocking permission during the tie. (4) spec.md:125 normatively says 'Permissions jump the queue'; the spec defines the formula but no tie-break, so this is a genuine boundary contradiction. (5) Not in the known-intentional list — none of the 8 items cover queue tie-breaking. (6) Severity 'minor' is honest: the window is at most ~60 seconds (after one full minute the permission scores 102 and outranks) and requires a >=20-minute-aged needs_input coexisting with a brand-new permission, but it misorders the queue top exactly when a permission (with an agent-side timeout) arrives. Suggested fix (status rank before statusSince) is correct and minimal.

confirmed.title: TUI queue order and scores go stale between events — aging bonus never triggers a re-broadcast
confirmed.description: The daemon broadcasts StatePush only when the registry reports a change (server.ts 'hook'/'respondPermission'/sweep paths). The agingBonus (+2/min) changes scores purely with time, and can reorder cross-status items (e.g. error 50 overtakes an aged-capped idle at 70 after ~10 min) — but with no events flowing, no push is sent, so the TUI keeps rendering the old order and scores indefinitely. The displayed "top item is 'the next thing'" (spec line 153) can disagree with what `holo next` (which rebuilds the queue daemon-side at request time, server.ts:202) would actually jump to. The TUI's 1s `now` tick only refreshes elapsed labels, not the daemon-supplied queue array.
confirmed.suggestion: Either have the daemon re-broadcast on a coarse timer when buildQueue output differs from the last push (piggyback on the existing 5s sweep), or ship statusSince-based re-scoring into the TUI so it re-sorts the queue locally on its 1s tick.

verdict.reasoning: Traced and confirmed. (1) Every broadcast() call in tui/src/daemon/server.ts is gated on a registry change: 'hook' broadcasts only if applyEvent returned changed (line 180-184), sweepOnce broadcasts only if reconcile||pruneExited returned true (lines 151-154), and registry.reconcile/pruneExited (registry.ts:178/191) return false in steady state — so with no events flowing, no StatePush is ever sent. There is no other daemon timer besides the sweep and permission-hold timeouts. (2) The aging reorder is concrete: scoring.ts gives +2/min capped at +40; an idle aged >=20min is capped at 70 while a fresher error (base 50) reaches 72 after 11 minutes, overtaking it in buildQueue's score-desc sort — purely time-driven, no events. (3) The TUI renders the daemon-supplied array verbatim: App.tsx line 90 `const queue = push?.queue ?? []`, QueuePane maps it in order; the 1s setNow tick (App.tsx 84-87) only feeds formatElapsed labels and PreviewPane, never re-scores/re-sorts; the gateway subscription is push-only with no polling. (4) 'next' (server.ts:201-212) rebuilds the queue at request time with this.now(), so it can jump to a different session than the TUI's displayed top item, contradicting spec.md:153 ('Top item is "the next thing"') until the next event happens to trigger a broadcast. (5) Not covered by any of the 8 known-intentional deviations, and no test or code implements aging-driven re-broadcast. Severity 'minor' is honest: it self-heals on any event, and Enter/a/d act on the selected sessionId so no wrong action results — it is a real but non-destructive staleness/consistency bug.

confirmed.title: Free-text cwd from the new-session modal is sent unresolved — relative paths and ~ break spawn
confirmed.description: Spec line 176 mandates the tab free-text path escape hatch. The modal submits the raw trimmed string (NewSessionModal.tsx:81-88, placeholder even advertises "/absolute/or/relative/path"), App passes it straight to {cmd:'new'}, and the daemon hands it to `tmux new-window -c <path>` and stores it verbatim in Session.cwd. A relative path resolves against the tmux server's cwd (not the TUI's), `~/...` is never expanded (no shell involved), and the bogus cwd then poisons Session.cwd, the diff-stat pane (`git -C <relative>`), and the recentCwds ranking. The CLI path does resolve (`resolve(cmd.cwd ?? process.cwd())`, cli.ts:209) — the TUI path doesn't.
confirmed.suggestion: Resolve in the TUI before submitting: expand a leading `~` with os.homedir() and apply path.resolve(); ideally also stat the directory and surface 'no such directory' via the modal's existing error line instead of spawning into a broken window.

verdict.reasoning: Traced end-to-end; the finding is real. NewSessionModal.tsx free mode submits the raw trimmed string (line 134 → submit() at 81-88; placeholder at 208 even advertises relative paths). App.tsx:171 forwards it verbatim in {cmd:'new'}; gateway/client are pure transports. Daemon handleNew (server.ts:271-282) stores it unmodified in Session.cwd via registry.createSession (registry.ts:55-72), pushes it into recentCwds (touchCwd, registry.ts:250-255), and passes it to RealTmux.newWindow which runs `tmux new-window -c <raw>` via execFile (tmux.ts:80-99) — no shell, so `~` is never expanded and a relative path is interpreted by the tmux server, not the TUI. The CLI path does resolve (cli.ts:209: resolve(cmd.cwd ?? process.cwd())), confirming the asymmetry. No validation exists anywhere in the chain, no tests cover free-text resolution, and this is not in the known-intentional list. Downstream poisoning is concrete: diffstat.ts:22 runs `git -C <bogus> diff --stat` (yields permanent 'no diff available' for ~ or wrong-base relative paths), and the bogus string is recycled into the cwd picker via recentCwds. One nuance: tmux's spawn falls back to $HOME (then /) when chdir to the -c path fails, so spawn usually succeeds silently in the wrong directory rather than failing outright — 'break spawn' is slightly overstated, but the agent running in $HOME while Session.cwd claims otherwise is the same defect with no error surfaced. Severity 'minor' is honest; suggested fix (expand ~, path.resolve, stat + modal error) is apt since the modal already has an error line.

confirmed.title: Preview pane's git diff --stat only refetches on selection change, not on session activity
confirmed.description: Spec lines 154 and 139-141: the preview shows git diff --stat so you can "often act without attaching". PreviewPane's effect is keyed on [cwd, diffStat] only (PreviewPane.tsx:31-46), so while a single session stays selected, the diff captured at selection time is never refreshed — an agent that keeps editing files and then stops shows the stale diff from minutes ago, undermining act-without-attaching for the review/idle case the preview exists for.
confirmed.suggestion: Add session.statusSince (or session.status) to the effect dependencies so the diff refetches whenever the selected session transitions state — cheap, and exactly the moments the user looks at the preview.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the code. PreviewPane.tsx:31-46 keys its git-diff effect on [cwd, diffStat] only. cwd is session?.cwd — a string unchanged while the same session stays selected (daemon pushes produce new session objects but identical cwd values, and effect deps compare by value). diffStat is referentially stable: App.tsx:41 defaults it to gitDiffStat, a module-level constant (diffstat.ts:37), and PreviewPane is rendered without a key prop so it never remounts. The 1s `now` tick re-renders but never re-runs the effect; status/lastMessage updates from daemon pushes render live while the diff stays frozen at selection time. Worst case is trivially reachable: with one session, effectiveId clamps selection to it permanently, so the diff is fetched once on the first daemon push and never again for the session's life — an agent that keeps editing and then stops shows the original stale diff next to a live status line, exactly undermining the spec's act-without-attaching goal (spec mockup lists git diff --stat; Preview/CONTEXT bullet says "enough to often act *without attaching*"). Not handled elsewhere: the daemon never computes diffs, there is no polling interval, and App.test.tsx only injects a fake runner without asserting refresh-on-activity. Not covered by any of the 8 known-intentional deviations. Severity "minor" is honest (display staleness, no crash), and the suggested fix (add session.statusSince/status to the deps) is cheap and targets the right moments.

confirmed.title: Harness configured flags are frozen at daemon startup — picker grays out harnesses installed later
confirmed.description: Spec line 175: unconfigured harnesses are "shown grayed, not hidden" — implying the grayed state reflects reality. `harnessInfos()` is awaited once at daemon startup (daemon/main.ts:17) and the resulting static array is served in every snapshot (server.ts:376). If the user installs claude/codex while holod is running, the modal still grays it out and `pick()` refuses it (NewSessionModal.tsx:70), even though the daemon's own `handleNew` re-checks `adapter.configured()` live and would happily spawn it. The inverse (uninstalled binary still shown configured) also misleads until spawn fails.
confirmed.suggestion: Re-probe configured-ness lazily — e.g. recompute harnessInfos during the periodic sweep or on each `new`/`subscribe`, caching with a short TTL since `which` probes are cheap.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by tracing the full chain; every factual claim in the finding holds.

1. Frozen at startup — CONFIRMED. /Users/ko/Development/holophyte/tui/src/daemon/main.ts:16 passes `harnesses: await harnessInfos()` once into the Daemon constructor. `harnessInfos()` (src/adapters/index.ts:22-29) is called nowhere else in the daemon; grep shows its only call sites are adapters/index.ts (definition), daemon/main.ts, and cli.ts (for the `holo ls` harness table, which probes fresh — making the TUI's staleness even more incongruous).

2. Static array served forever — CONFIRMED. server.ts:371-379 `snapshot()` returns `harnesses: this.opts.harnesses` on every `ls`, `subscribe`, and broadcast. The comment at server.ts:34 ("precomputed configured flags — avoids re-probing binaries per snapshot") shows it was a deliberate perf choice, but nothing ever refreshes it — not the 5s sweep (sweepOnce, server.ts:146-155, only reconciles tmux windows), not handleNew.

3. configured() is genuinely dynamic — CONFIRMED. adapters/claude.ts:75 and codex.ts:39 default to `spawnSync('which', [bin]).status === 0`, so the real value changes when binaries are installed/removed mid-run. (cursor/devin stubs are hardcoded false, fake is static — the staleness only matters for claude/codex, exactly as the finding scopes it.)

4. Picker hard-blocks — CONFIRMED. NewSessionModal.tsx:70 `pick()` returns early on `!h?.configured`, and line ~186 renders "○ not configured". A harness installed after daemon start is unreachable via the TUI until holod restarts.

5. Daemon inconsistency — CONFIRMED. server.ts:264 `handleNew` re-checks `adapter.configured()` live, so `holo new codex` via the CLI (cli.ts:80, sends the `new` request directly) succeeds for a newly installed harness while the TUI picker refuses it. The inverse (binary removed mid-run) shows configured in the picker and fails at handleNew with "harness not configured" — exactly the "misleads until spawn fails" the finding describes.

Not covered by any of the 8 known-intentional deviations. Severity "minor" is honest: workarounds exist (restart holod, or use the CLI directly), and mid-daemon installs are infrequent — but the daemon is long-lived (survives TUI quits), so the stale flag persists indefinitely. One soft spot: spec line 175 only literally says "shown grayed, not hidden"; the freshness expectation is an inference. But the concrete UI-vs-daemon disagreement (picker refuses what handleNew would accept) is a real, reachable defect regardless of spec wording. The suggested fix (re-probe on sweep or per-new/subscribe with a short TTL) is proportionate since the probe is a cheap `which`.

confirmed.title: Claude /clear (SessionEnd reason 'clear'/'resume') permanently kills tracking of a live session
confirmed.description: map.ts maps EVERY SessionEnd to {kind:'exit'} regardless of reason, but the project's own research doc (tui/docs/hooks-research.md) documents reasons 'clear' and 'resume', which fire when the user runs /clear (or /resume) INSIDE a still-running claude process — the process and tmux window stay alive and a SessionStart(source:'clear') follows immediately. Concrete failure: user jumps into a holo-managed claude window and types /clear. The hook sends 'exit' → registry.terminate() sets status 'exited'. The follow-up SessionStart 'ready' event is rejected because acceptEvent() refuses anything on an exited session ('nothing revives an exited session' is a tested invariant, registry.test.ts:217), and so is every later prompt/tool/stop/permission event. After 60s the sweep's pruneExited() deletes the session entirely; all subsequent hook events hit 'unknown session' and are dropped. Result: an actively running agent silently vanishes from the sessions list and the attention queue forever — the exact thing holo exists to prevent. The known-deviations list does not cover this.
confirmed.suggestion: In mapHook's SessionEnd case, return {type:'ignore'} when payload.reason is 'clear' or 'resume' (the subsequent SessionStart already re-emits 'ready'); keep mapping 'logout', 'prompt_input_exit', 'bypass_permissions_disabled', 'other' (and missing reason) to exit. The tmux liveness sweep remains the backstop if the process actually dies. Add map.test.ts cases for reason:'clear' and reason:'resume'.

verdict.reasoning: Traced end-to-end and confirmed. (1) map.ts:83-94 maps every Claude SessionEnd to {kind:'exit'} with no reason check. (2) The project's own verified research doc (docs/hooks-research.md lines 18, 23) documents SessionEnd reasons 'clear' and 'resume' and SessionStart source 'clear' — /clear fires SessionEnd(clear) then SessionStart(clear) inside the same still-running process. (3) The scenario is reachable: adapters/claude.ts registers the SessionEnd hook with the holo sessionId baked into the per-session --settings file, so post-/clear hooks reuse the same holo sessionId. (4) server.ts 'hook' → registry.applyEvent → 'exit' → terminate(status 'exited'). (5) registry.ts acceptEvent rejects ALL events on an exited session — the registry test 'nothing revives an exited session' explicitly includes {kind:'ready'}, so the follow-up SessionStart is dropped. (6) The 5s sweep's pruneExited (60s grace) then deletes the session; all later hook events hit unknown-session and are silently dropped (server always acks ok:true). No revival path exists: reconcile only terminates, sessions are only created via the explicit 'new' command, and the tmux liveness backstop is useless here because the window is still alive — the bug is a false exit. Not covered by any of the 8 known-intentional deviations; map.test.ts only tests reason 'prompt_input_exit'/non-string/codex-ignore, never 'clear'/'resume'. Severity is honest: a live agent permanently vanishes from the attention queue after a routine action, and subsequent permission requests silently degrade to in-pane-only — defeating the tool's core purpose. The suggested fix (ignore SessionEnd when reason is 'clear'/'resume'; the follow-up SessionStart re-emits 'ready') is correct and minimal.

confirmed.title: onJsonLines decodes each socket chunk independently — multi-byte UTF-8 split at chunk boundaries is corrupted
confirmed.description: onJsonLines does `buf += chunk.toString()` on raw Buffers (grep confirms no setEncoding anywhere in tui/src). Buffer.toString() decodes each chunk in isolation, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character straddling a read boundary becomes U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides. JSON.stringify does not escape non-ASCII, so CJK/emoji/accented text travels as raw multi-byte sequences. Any NDJSON message larger than one kernel read (~64KB) is delivered in multiple 'data' events with arbitrary byte split points. Concrete failure: a Claude PermissionRequest for a Write tool carrying a >64KB file with non-ASCII content — the hook→daemon permission line gets split mid-character; the stored pendingPermission.input (and the StatePush broadcast of it to the TUI, same code path) shows mangled � text, so the user approves a permission whose displayed input is silently corrupted. Same risk for large StatePush snapshots (many sessions × 2000-char lastMessages) on the TUI subscription socket. JSON.parse still succeeds (U+FFFD is a valid string char), so the corruption is silent.
confirmed.suggestion: Call socket.setEncoding('utf8') at the top of onJsonLines (Node then uses string_decoder internally, which carries partial sequences across chunks), or accumulate Buffers and decode with a StringDecoder. Add a test that writes one JSON line containing a multi-byte char in two chunks split mid-character.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. Traced end to end and reproduced the corruption empirically.

Mechanics (confirmed): /Users/ko/Development/holophyte/tui/src/ndjson.ts:13-14 does `socket.on('data', (chunk) => { buf += chunk.toString() })`. Grep confirms no `setEncoding` or `StringDecoder` anywhere in tui/src, so 'data' delivers raw Buffers and each is decoded in isolation. I ran the exact ndjson.ts decode logic against a JSON line split mid-character ('日' split after its first byte): result was `"���本語テスト"` — and JSON.parse SUCCEEDED, confirming the corruption is silent (U+FFFD lands inside string values; JSON structural chars are single-byte ASCII and can never themselves be split). The StringDecoder control decoded correctly. Non-ASCII does travel raw: JSON.stringify does not escape it.

Reachability (confirmed): The permission path carries untruncated tool input — map.ts:96-101 passes `payload.tool_input` verbatim, hook/main.ts:100-111 sends it as one NDJSON line, and the daemon reads it via onJsonLines at server.ts:163. A Claude Write/Edit PermissionRequest with a >64KB file (Node's default read chunk) is guaranteed to arrive in multiple 'data' events with arbitrary byte boundaries. The corrupted input is then stored (registry.ts:150 `session.pendingPermission = { tool, input, respondBy }`) and re-broadcast in full StatePush snapshots (server.ts:385) over a second onJsonLines hop (client.ts:34, :83), where a >64KB snapshot can split inside any session's lastMessage/question text — which PreviewPane.tsx:92 renders as full lines. Not in the known-intentional list; zero test coverage (no ndjson test file exists; server.test.ts has no chunk/split/encoding tests). The suggested fix (setEncoding('utf8') or StringDecoder) is correct — verified the StringDecoder path produces clean output.

Two honest caveats on severity framing: (1) The finding's headline example — "user approves a permission whose displayed input shows mangled text" — is overstated in one detail: PreviewPane.tsx:77 displays only the first 200 chars (MAX_INPUT_CHARS=200) of the stringified input, while the first split boundary of a >64KB message is ~64KB in, so corruption almost never appears in that visible prefix. The user-visible corruption surface is instead lastMessage/question text in large StatePush snapshots, plus corrupted stored daemon state. (2) Corruption never changes what the harness actually executes — the daemon only returns allow/deny and the harness uses its own original input — so this is display/state fidelity corruption, not action corruption. 'Major' is at the aggressive end; minor-to-major is fairer. But the defect itself is concrete, reachable, silent, and untested: the finding stands.

confirmed.title: request() never settles when the peer closes without replying — daemon crash mid-hold freezes the agent's permission dialog for ~95s
confirmed.description: request() settles only on (a) first JSON line, (b) 'error' event, or (c) its own timer. A clean EOF (peer closed, no data) emits 'end'/'close' but NOT 'error', so the promise just hangs until the timer. Graceful daemon stop is fine (releaseHold replies 'timeout' first), but if holod is SIGKILLed / OOM-killed / crashes while holding a permission connection, the hook process's socket gets a clean FIN and request() sits until PERMISSION_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_MS = 95000. Per the research doc, Claude's permission dialog does not appear until the PermissionRequest hook process exits — so the agent's permission prompt is frozen for up to ~95 seconds after the daemon died, violating hook/main.ts's own 'never block the agent' hard requirement (the intended degradation was immediate fall-through to the in-pane dialog). The same gap delays fake-agent permission steps and adds up to 1-2s stalls to ordinary event hooks when the daemon dies mid-request.
confirmed.suggestion: In request(), add socket.once('close', ...) (or 'end') that clears the timer and rejects with 'connection closed before response' if the promise is still pending. tryRequest/hook main already swallow the rejection and exit 0, restoring the instant in-pane fallback.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. Every link in the finding's chain checks out against the code, plus an empirical reproduction of the crux.

1. confirmed.title: Stale-socket takeover race in Daemon.start() can yield two live daemons fighting over state.json
confirmed.description: start() does: existsSync(socket) → ping (250ms) → unlinkSync → listen, with no lock serializing check-and-bind. After a daemon crash leaves a stale socket file, two CLIs launched near-simultaneously (e.g. `holo ls` in a script while `holo` runs interactively) both fail the ensureDaemon ping and both spawn daemons. Interleaving: A sees stale socket, ping ECONNREFUSED, unlinks, listens (creates fresh socket). B, having passed its own existsSync+ping against the stale file moments earlier, then unlinks — removing A's LIVE socket — and listen() succeeds on the now-free path. Result: two daemons running; A is orphaned (its socket file gone, unreachable, never told to stop) yet keeps its sweep timer and persists its restored registry to the same state.json that B writes, so the two overwrite each other (and both use the same `state.json.tmp`, risking a torn rename). Sessions spawned via B are silently clobbered in the file by A's periodic saves. Same 250ms-ping false-negative against a busy live daemon triggers the identical takeover.
confirmed.suggestion: Bind first and treat EADDRINUSE as 'maybe alive': on EADDRINUSE, ping; if dead, unlink and retry listen once. Or guard the whole check-unlink-listen with an O_EXCL lock file (e.g. holod.lock containing the pid) and have the orphan detect socket-file loss in its sweep and self-terminate.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED — the race is concrete and reachable as described.

Code trace (/Users/ko/Development/holophyte/tui/src/daemon/server.ts:73-109): `start()` does exactly `existsSync(socketFile)` → `tryRequest({cmd:'ping'},{timeoutMs:250})` → if live throw 'holod already running' → `unlinkSync(socketFile)` (failure swallowed) → `listen(socketFile)`. There is no lock file, no pid file, and no serialization between check/unlink and bind — TOCTOU across processes.

Dual-spawn precondition is real: `makeEnsureDaemon` (/Users/ko/Development/holophyte/tui/src/cli.ts:302-341) pings (300ms), and on failure unconditionally `spawnDetached`s a daemon, with no lock either. Two CLIs racing against a stale socket (left by a crash/SIGKILL — `doStop` only unlinks on clean stop) both fail the ping and both spawn daemons A and B, which then run `start()` concurrently.

The claimed interleaving works: connecting to a listener-less unix socket file yields fast ECONNREFUSED (client.ts:27-30 rejects, tryRequest returns null → falsy `live`). A: ping-fail → unlink stale → listen (binds fresh path). B: its ping completed against the stale file before A's listen (so no 'already running' throw), then its `unlinkSync` executes after A's listen — removing A's LIVE socket file. Unix-socket bind fails EADDRINUSE only if the path exists, so B's listen on the now-free path succeeds. A's bound socket survives unlink (open inode) so A stays alive but unreachable — node doesn't watch the path, and `sweepOnce` (server.ts:146-155) only reconciles tmux windows; there is no socket-loss self-check. The 250ms-timeout false negative against a busy live daemon triggers the same takeover (timeout → tryRequest null → treated as dead → unlink live socket).

Consequences check out: both daemons captured the same `statePath()` (paths.ts) and `saveStateFile` (state-file.ts:41-47) uses the shared `state.json.tmp`; A's sweep persists whenever reconcile/prune change anything (window closed, 60s exited-prune), overwriting the file with a registry lacking B's sessions — so B's spawned sessions are clobbered on disk exactly as claimed. Concurrent writes to the same tmp path can also produce corrupt published content ("torn rename" is slightly loose wording — rename is atomic, the tmp content is what can interleave — but the substance is right). Bonus hazard not even claimed: if orphan A is later SIGTERMed, doStop's `unlinkSync(socketFile)` deletes B's socket.

Not handled elsewhere: server.test.ts only covers the live-daemon refusal path ('holod already running', line ~184); no stale-socket race test. Not in the 8 known-intentional deviations. Severity 'minor' is honest — needs a crash-left stale socket plus near-simultaneous launches (or a >250ms event-loop stall in a live daemon), a narrow window, but with real split-brain/state-clobber consequences. The suggested fixes (bind-first with EADDRINUSE→ping→retry, or O_EXCL lock file + orphan self-termination) are sound.

confirmed.title: Mid-spawn crash can persist a session with tmuxWindow '' that nothing ever cleans up
confirmed.description: handleNew creates the session (tmuxWindow: '') and only assigns the window id after awaiting adapter.spawnCommand() and tmux.newWindow(). During those awaits any other request (e.g. a hook event from another session) triggers persist(), writing the half-created session with tmuxWindow '' to state.json. If the daemon dies before setTmuxWindow, the restored registry contains a phantom: reconcile() explicitly skips sessions with tmuxWindow === '' (registry.ts) so the liveness sweep never marks it exited, pruneExited only removes exited sessions, and there is no kill/remove command — it sits in the queue as idle 'awaiting first prompt' forever, and 'jump'/Enter selects window '' (a no-op tmux error). Concrete scenario: holod crashes (or is SIGKILLed) during a slow tmux new-window while a fake/claude hook event lands → permanent ghost queue item after restart.
confirmed.suggestion: Treat tmuxWindow === '' as dead during restore (drop it or mark exited in SessionRegistry.fromJSON, mirroring the permission demotion), or have reconcile() terminate sessions whose tmuxWindow is '' and whose createdAt is older than a few seconds.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing tui/src/daemon/server.ts and registry.ts. (1) handleNew (server.ts:271-282) inserts the session into the registry with tmuxWindow:'' (registry.ts:62,71) BEFORE awaiting adapter.spawnCommand() and tmux.newWindow() — both real async gaps (fs writes; execFile tmux subprocess). (2) During that window, persist() can write the half-created session to state.json: hook requests from other sessions (server.ts:181), handlePermission's unconditional persist (server.ts:343), the 5s sweep, and — most directly — SIGTERM→doStop() persists unconditionally (server.ts:137) then process.exit(0) (main.ts:30) kills the in-flight handleNew, so even graceful shutdown mid-spawn writes the phantom with no concurrent request needed. (3) The removeSession error path (server.ts:284) only runs if newWindow throws while the daemon lives — not on daemon death. (4) On restart, fromJSON (registry.ts:29-45) restores it as-is (only 'permission' status is special-cased). (5) Nothing cleans it: reconcile explicitly skips tmuxWindow==='' (registry.ts:185, behavior locked in by registry.test.ts:468 'skips sessions without a window'); pruneExited only drops status==='exited' (registry.ts:196); protocol.ts has no kill/remove command; no hook can ever target it since its harnessSessionId was never given to any spawned harness, so applyEvent's exit path is unreachable. (6) idle scores 30 in scoring.ts so it sits in the queue forever; jump runs selectWindow('') — tmux select-window -t '' fails silently (tmux.ts resolves non-zero status) yet replies ok:true. Not in the known-intentional list (deviation #8 is about live spawned sessions, not persistence of half-created ones across daemon death). Severity 'minor' is honest: low-probability trigger (daemon death inside the spawn window) but permanent consequence with zero in-app remediation short of hand-editing ~/.holo/state.json. One immaterial nit: the phantom's attentionReason would be 'starting…' (ready never fired), not 'awaiting first prompt'. The suggested fix (drop or mark-exited tmuxWindow==='' sessions in fromJSON, mirroring the permission demotion) is correct — at restore time no spawn can be in flight, so a restored '' window is definitionally dead.

confirmed.title: `holo next` exits 0 on genuine daemon/tmux errors, not just on an empty queue
confirmed.description: The 'next' case treats every {ok:false} response as the benign 'queue is empty' situation: it prints res.error to stdout and returns 0. But the daemon's handleLine catch wraps real failures in {ok:false, error} too — e.g. tmux binary missing (selectWindow rejection) or any thrown error while jumping. Concrete scenario: tmux is not installed / the holo session's window was killed mid-jump → `holo next` prints the error to stdout (not stderr) and exits 0, so scripts and the user's shell see success. Compare the 'new' and 'ls' cases, which correctly route errors to stderr with exit 1.
confirmed.suggestion: Make the daemon distinguish the empty-queue case (e.g. reply {ok:true} with no session, or a dedicated error code/string the CLI matches exactly); in the CLI, exit 0 with a stdout message only for that case and otherwise stderr + exit 1.

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the code. cli.ts 'next' (lines 222-236) routes every {ok:false} response to stdout with exit 0 — it never distinguishes the daemon's benign 'queue is empty' error (server.ts:206) from genuine failures, while the 'new' and 'ls' cases correctly use stderr + exit 1. The daemon's onConnection catch-all (server.ts:163-167) wraps any rejection in handleLine as {ok:false, error: String(err)}, and the 'next' handler awaits tmux.selectWindow (server.ts:209), so real exceptions reach the CLI in the same envelope as the empty queue. Reachable concrete path: daemon running, tmux binary removed afterwards (e.g. brew/nix swap) → execFile rejects ENOENT (tmux.ts defaultRunner rejects only on ENOENT) → {ok:false, error:'Error: spawn tmux ENOENT'} → `holo next` prints it to stdout and exits 0. Caveats that narrow but don't refute the finding: (1) the 'window killed mid-jump' sub-scenario is mischaracterized — RealTmux.selectWindow ignores non-zero exit status, so that case yields a silent {ok:true} 'jumped to...' false success, not an {ok:false}; (2) cold-start tmux-missing never reaches this branch because daemon start fails at sweepOnce → ensureDaemon throws → top-level await rejects → non-zero exit. Not in the known-intentional list; the only test (cli.test.ts:551) covers the literal 'queue is empty' string, not arbitrary errors, and the '// queue empty is not an error' comment shows intent for the benign case only. Severity 'minor' is honest; the suggested protocol-level fix (e.g. {ok:true} with no session for empty queue) is sound.

confirmed.title: Daemon crash while a permission is held freezes the agent for up to 95s — client.request() never settles on socket close
confirmed.description: request() settles only on a 'data' line (resolve) or an 'error' event (reject). When the daemon process is SIGKILLed or crashes from an unhandled error while holding N PermissionRequest connections, the kernel sends a clean FIN: the hook's socket gets 'end'/'close' with NO 'error' event, so the promise stays pending until the client-side timer fires — PERMISSION_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_MS = 95_000 in hook/main.ts. Claude's permission dialog cannot appear until the hook process exits (docs/hooks-research.md), so the user sees a frozen agent with no dialog and no holo UI (daemon is dead) for ~95 seconds, per held permission. This defeats the exact degradation path the spec mandates ('daemon down → hook exits silently → in-pane prompt'): that path is fast only for connect-refused, not for mid-hold crashes. Graceful stop() is fine (releaseHold replies 'timeout' first); only the crash path is broken — which is precisely when robustness matters.
confirmed.suggestion: In request(), add a settled flag and socket.once('close', ...) that clears the timer and rejects (or resolves null) if no response line arrived. The held permission hook then exits 0 with no output immediately on daemon death and the in-pane dialog appears within milliseconds. Add a server.test/e2e case: hold a permission, destroy the daemon's server socket without replying, assert the hook-side request settles promptly.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the actual code. (1) client.ts request() (lines 21-39) settles only on a response line ('data' via onJsonLines), an 'error' event, or the timeout timer — there is no 'end'/'close' handler. The adjacent subscribe() function DOES handle socket.on('close'), confirming the omission in request(). (2) daemon/main.ts installs handlers only for SIGINT/SIGTERM; SIGKILL or an uncaught exception kills holod without releaseHold() replies, so held hook sockets receive a clean EOF ('end'/'close', no 'error') and the promise stays pending. (3) hook/main.ts uses timeoutMs: PERMISSION_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_MS = 95_000 for the permission request; the timer is not unref'd, so the hook process hangs ~95s before exiting 0. (4) docs/hooks-research.md:28 confirms 'the permission dialog does not appear until the hook process exits', and adapters/claude.ts sets PERMISSION_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SEC = 150, deliberately above the daemon hold, so Claude will not kill the hook earlier — the agent is genuinely frozen with no dialog for ~95s per held permission. (5) spec.md:62 and :112 mandate the fast silent-exit degradation path for daemon-down; connect-refused fails fast via 'error' (ECONNREFUSED) but mid-hold crash does not. (6) Not handled elsewhere: graceful doStop() replies 'timeout' before ending sockets (the finding correctly concedes this path is fine); server.test.ts:471 tests only the reverse direction (hook socket destroyed while daemon holds); e2e.test.ts uses SIGTERM (graceful). No test covers daemon hard-death mid-hold from the hook side. (7) Not in the known-intentional deviations list. Severity 'major' is honest: requires an abnormal daemon death, but produces a silently frozen agent for ~95s in precisely the crash scenario the degradation path exists for, and the fix (settle on 'close', as subscribe() already does) is small and matches existing patterns.

confirmed.title: /clear and in-app /resume permanently orphan a live Claude session (SessionEnd reason ignored; exited sessions can't be revived)
confirmed.description: mapHook maps every SessionEnd to {kind:'exit'} regardless of payload.reason. Per docs/hooks-research.md, Claude fires SessionEnd with reason 'clear' (user types /clear) and 'resume' (switching conversations in-process) — cases where the claude process and tmux window stay alive. registry.applyEvent terminates the session ('exited'), the follow-up SessionStart(source=clear|resume) → 'ready' is rejected by acceptEvent ('nothing revives an exited session', registry.ts:211), and pruneExited deletes the session 60s later. Result: a running agent in a live tmux window that holo no longer tracks — all subsequent hook events hit an unknown session id and are silently acked-and-ignored (server.ts 'always ack fast, even unknown session'). The user is back to scanning panes, the exact failure the product exists to prevent, and /clear is an everyday command. Related: SessionStart(source=compact) fires mid-turn after auto-compaction and maps to 'ready' → session flips to idle/'awaiting first prompt' and produces a phantom queue item while the agent is still working, until the next PreToolUse corrects it.
confirmed.suggestion: Inspect the discriminator fields in map.ts: for SessionEnd, treat reason 'clear' and 'resume' as 'ignore' (or map to a non-terminal event) since the process survives; only 'logout', 'prompt_input_exit', 'bypass_permissions_disabled', 'other' mean the process is going away (the tmux liveness sweep already backstops real exits). For SessionStart, ignore source 'compact'. Optionally also let registry.applyEvent revive a not-yet-pruned 'exited' session on 'ready' as defense in depth.

verdict.reasoning: Verified end-to-end by reading the code. (1) map.ts:83-94 maps every SessionEnd to {kind:'exit'} regardless of payload.reason, and map.ts:39-40 maps every SessionStart to {kind:'ready'} regardless of source. (2) The project's own research doc (tui/docs/hooks-research.md:18,23, verified against Claude Code 2.1.170) lists SessionEnd reasons clear|resume|... and SessionStart sources including clear/compact — /clear and in-app resume are in-process, so the claude process and tmux window survive. (3) The scenario is concrete: adapters/claude.ts:35-38 bakes the holo session id into the injected hook argv and the --settings hooks are process-level, so post-/clear hooks keep firing at the same holo session id. SessionEnd(clear) → exit → registry.ts:132-133 terminate('exited'); the follow-up SessionStart(clear) → ready is rejected by acceptEvent (registry.ts:213 'nothing revives an exited session'); reconcile skips exited sessions (registry.ts:184) so window liveness can't help; pruneExited (registry.ts:193-203, swept every 5s per server.ts:146-155) deletes the session after 60s. Thereafter all hook events for that id are acked-and-ignored (server.ts:179 'always ack fast, even unknown session') and permission requests degrade to in-pane dialogs (server.ts:321-324) — a live, working agent in a live tmux window that holo permanently stopped tracking. (4) Not handled elsewhere: map.test.ts only tests reason 'prompt_input_exit' and non-string reasons; no revival/adoption path exists in daemon/cli. (5) Not in the known-intentional list (items 1-8 don't cover SessionEnd reasons); spec.md:58's rationale ('covers Ctrl+C') shows clear/resume wasn't considered. (6) The compact sub-claim is also real: SessionStart(compact) → ready flips a running session to idle/'awaiting first prompt' (registry.ts:112-113) and idle scores 30 in scoring.ts (queue-eligible), creating a phantom queue item until the next PreToolUse. Severity 'major' is honest: /clear is an everyday command and the result is unrecoverable loss of tracking — the exact failure the product exists to prevent.

confirmed.title: Duplicate-daemon takeover: ping-then-unlink TOCTOU in Daemon.start() plus ensureDaemon spawn-on-timeout can orphan a live daemon and clobber state.json
confirmed.description: start() (lines 80-99) does existsSync → ping (250ms timeout) → unlinkSync → listen. Two interleavings produce TWO running daemons: (1) stale-socket race — after a daemon crash, two concurrent `holo` invocations both ping the dead socket, A unlinks and listens (recreating the file), then B's already-scheduled unlink deletes A's LIVE socket and B listens successfully; (2) busy-daemon takeover — under machine load (N parallel agents compiling is the product's normal operating mode) the live daemon misses the 300ms ping in makeEnsureDaemon (cli.ts:317), the CLI spawns a second daemon, whose own 250ms ping also times out, so it unlinks the live socket and takes over. In both cases the orphaned daemon keeps running invisibly: it still holds any in-flight permission connections (agents wait on a daemon nobody can reach), its sweep keeps running against the same tmux server, it persists to the SAME state.json (last-writer-wins clobbering the active daemon's sessions/counters), and an already-connected TUI subscription stays attached to the orphan, displaying stale state indefinitely while hooks flow to the new daemon.
confirmed.suggestion: Hold an exclusive lock for the daemon's lifetime — e.g. open ~/.holo/holod.lock with O_CREAT|O_EXCL semantics via proper-lockfile-style flock, or write the pid and verify after listen by re-stat()ing the socket path and confirming it is the inode this server bound (bail if not). In makeEnsureDaemon, never spawn on a ping timeout alone — retry the ping a couple of times with backoff first, and have the TUI re-subscribe when it sees pushes stop while ping succeeds.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED against the code. The mechanism, the takeover path, and every claimed consequence except one detail check out.

The core TOCTOU is exactly as described (tui/src/daemon/server.ts:80-99): start() does existsSync → tryRequest ping with timeoutMs 250 → unlinkSync → listen. There is no lock file, no post-listen inode verification, and grep confirms no locking anywhere in tui/src or spec.md. The only single-instance guard is the ping, and the only test (server.test.ts:181-184) covers just the happy path where the live daemon answers the ping in time.

Scenario 2 (busy-daemon takeover) is the concrete, reachable one. makeEnsureDaemon (cli.ts:314-321) spawns a detached daemon on a single failed 300ms ping — no retry/backoff. The new daemon's own 250ms ping (server.ts:82) then has to be answered by the same loaded daemon; the two misses are correlated (same machine load), not independent. On miss, unlinkSync deletes the LIVE daemon's socket path and listen() succeeds on the now-free path — net.Server bound to an unlinked unix-socket inode keeps running with no error, so the orphan never notices. ensureDaemon runs on every `holo attach/new/next/ls` invocation, and the product's normal operating mode is N parallel agents loading the machine, so exposure is recurring.

Scenario 1 (stale-socket race) is technically real as written — B's ping can resolve as dead before A listens, and B's subsequent unlinkSync then deletes A's freshly-bound socket — but the window between B's ping rejection and B's unlinkSync is sub-millisecond, so on its own this would be minor. The common interleavings are already handled by EADDRINUSE (one daemon exits) or by the ping answering ('holod already running'). Scenario 2 carries the severity.

Consequences verified in code:
- Same state.json clobbering: both daemons persist via saveStateFile to statePath() (server.ts:393-395, paths.ts:17-19); writes are atomic per-write (tmp+rename, state-file.ts:41-47) but uncoordinated — last-writer-wins between the orphan's sweep/permission-timeout persists and the new daemon's. Confirmed.
- Orphan keeps sweeping the same tmux server: sweepTimer (server.ts:103-108) never stops; nothing re-checks socket ownership after listen. Confirmed.
- TUI stuck on the orphan: subscribe() (client.ts:67-92) only fires onClose when the socket drops; the orphan stays alive so onClose never fires and App.tsx's retry-on-close never triggers. Worse — verified that respondPermission goes through gateway.request → a FRESH connection to socketPath() (App.tsx:155, client.ts:22), i.e. to the NEW daemon, which replies 'no pending permission' (server.ts:231-236). So during a takeover the TUI displays the orphan's pending permission but cannot answer it. Confirmed.
- One overstatement: 'agents wait on a daemon nobody can reach' is bounded, not indefinite — the daemon-side hold caps at permissionMaxHoldMs (90s default, server.ts:308) and then replies 'timeout', making the hook fall through to the in-pane dialog. Remote approval is broken for up to 90s per request, not forever.

Not in the known-intentional list (items 1-8 don't touch daemon lifecycle). No test exercises the ping-timeout/unlink path. Severity 'major' is honest: silent split-brain in the daemon whose entire job is being the single source of truth for live agent state, triggered by the product's normal operating condition (loaded machine), with state-file corruption and a permanently-stale TUI as outcomes. The suggested fixes (lifetime lock with O_EXCL/flock, post-listen inode re-stat, ping retry with backoff before spawning) are appropriate.

confirmed.title: One spurious tmux list-windows failure permanently destroys all session tracking
confirmed.description: listWindowIds() returns [] for ANY non-zero status (line 119), and defaultRunner maps every non-ENOENT execFile error — including EAGAIN/EMFILE fork failures under load — to a non-zero status (line 32). The 5s sweep then runs registry.reconcile([]), which marks every session 'exited'/'window closed'; acceptEvent refuses to revive exited sessions, and pruneExited deletes them 60s later. So a single transient subprocess-spawn failure (process-table pressure from many agents, tmux server briefly restarting, fd exhaustion) silently and irreversibly converts a healthy board of live agents into an empty registry, while the tmux windows and agents keep running — their hooks thereafter ack into unknown session ids. The trigger probability is low-moderate, but it scales with exactly the load the tool is built for, and recovery requires noticing and mentally re-mapping every window.
confirmed.suggestion: Distinguish 'session/server gone' from 'could not ask': have defaultRunner reject (or return a sentinel) on spawn-level errors, and have listWindowIds throw so sweepOnce's existing catch skips reconcile for that tick. Additionally require 2-3 consecutive empty/failed sweeps before terminating sessions, and/or revive a not-yet-pruned exited session whose tmuxWindow reappears in a later sweep.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the code. (1) tmux.ts:27-32: defaultRunner rejects only on code==='ENOENT'; Node execFile reports spawn-level failures (EAGAIN/EMFILE/ENOMEM) with string error codes, which resolve as { status: 1 }. (2) tmux.ts:118: listWindowIds returns [] for ANY non-zero status — the comment and test (tmux.test.ts:186) show [] was meant for "session gone", conflating it with "could not ask". (3) server.ts:146-150: sweepOnce feeds the [] directly into registry.reconcile, which (registry.ts:180-190) terminates every non-exited session with a window as 'exited'/'window closed'. (4) registry.ts:213 acceptEvent blocks revival ("nothing revives an exited session"), reconcile has no revive path, and pruneExited (registry.ts:193-203) deletes after 60s grace — guaranteed by the 5s sweep — with persist() overwriting the state file, so the loss is irreversible. The interval's .catch (server.ts:104) already skips the tick on rejection (ENOENT today), confirming the suggested fix mechanism works. One caveat: the finding's "tmux server briefly restarting" trigger is wrong — tmux panes are children of the server, so a server death kills the agents and marking sessions exited would be correct; the real triggers are daemon-side fork/fd failures (EAGAIN/EMFILE in holod) and transient tmux client connect failures while the server lives. Probability is genuinely low (the finding honestly says low-moderate), but the consequence — silent, total, unrecoverable registry destruction from one bad sample of a fallible read on a 5s timer — makes "major" defensible. Not in the known-intentional list and not mitigated elsewhere.

confirmed.title: Concurrent PermissionRequests on one session: replaced hold plus masked Notification leaves the session stuck 'running' while the pane is blocked on a dialog
confirmed.description: handlePermission (line 311) resolves an existing hold as 'timeout' when a second permission arrives for the same session — the first hook exits with no output and Claude shows its in-pane dialog, firing Notification(permission_prompt). But at that moment the session status is 'permission' (second hold), so registry.applyEvent masks the notification (registry.ts:99-107) while still advancing lastEventTs — the event is permanently lost, not deferred. When the user remotely approves the second permission, resolvePermission sets the session to 'running', yet the pane is actually frozen on the first tool's dialog. No further hooks fire while it's blocked, so the session displays 'running' indefinitely, never queues, and the blocked dialog is invisible until the user happens to attach — a silent attention leak in an attention-queue tool. Requires Claude to fire overlapping PermissionRequest hooks for parallel tool calls (unverified frequency; the code comment already assumes it can happen).
confirmed.suggestion: Don't replace the existing hold: reply 'timeout' to the NEW permission request instead, so the newer tool degrades to the in-pane dialog while the held one stays remotely answerable — and the subsequent Notification then lands on a non-permission status. Alternatively key holds by sessionId+tool_use_id and let resolvePermission fall back to 'needs_input: permission prompt in pane' when other holds/dialogs are known to be outstanding. Verify Claude's actual behavior with two parallel permission-requiring tool calls and encode it in a server.test case.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the full chain through the actual code. (1) server.ts:311-313 replaces an existing hold by resolving it 'timeout' when a second permission arrives — the comment confirms overlapping PermissionRequests are an assumed-possible case (the branch exists only for it). (2) hook/main.ts:112-126: a 'timeout' decision produces no stdout, so Claude falls through to the in-pane dialog; tui/docs/hooks-research.md explicitly documents (as verified ground truth) that Notification(permission_prompt) then fires. (3) The masking is deterministic, not racy: beginPermission for the second tool runs synchronously in the same handlePermission tick, so status is 'permission' again before the Notification hook (a fresh process spawn) can possibly deliver its event; registry.ts:96-109 then drops the notification while acceptEvent (line 214) advances lastEventTs — the event is lost, not deferred. (4) On remote approval of the second hold, resolvePermission (registry.ts:172-175) sets status 'running' with no attentionReason, while the pane is actually frozen on the first tool's dialog. (5) No recovery: PostToolUse is unmapped (map.ts default → ignore), Stop can't fire while the turn is blocked, the Notification fired once and was eaten, and scoring.ts excludes 'running' from the queue — so the session is invisible to the attention queue indefinitely; only manual attach or window death (sweep) escapes. (6) The existing test (server.test.ts:416) covers replacement + remote approve but never injects the intervening Notification, so the failure state is untested. (7) Not in the known-intentional deviations list. The finding's one disclosed uncertainty — whether Claude actually fires overlapping PermissionRequest hooks — is fair, but the code is explicitly written for that precondition, and conditional on it the failure is concrete and reachable. Severity 'minor' is honest (rare trigger, but silently defeats the tool's core attention-queue promise). Suggested fixes are sound; tool_use_id is available per the research doc.

confirmed.title: HOLO_HOME / HOLO_TMUX_SESSION are not propagated to tmux-spawned hooks and TUI — non-default homes silently misroute events
confirmed.description: hookCommand() embeds only the bun path, hook script path, harness, and session id. The hook process inherits the TMUX SERVER's environment (not the daemon's), so with a custom HOLO_HOME (or HOLO_TMUX_SESSION) the daemon listens on $HOLO_HOME/holod.sock while injected claude/codex hooks connect to ~/.holo/holod.sock — tryRequest fails (or worse, reaches a DIFFERENT daemon, which acks the unknown session id and drops the event). The session then sits at 'idle / awaiting first prompt' forever with zero error surfaced anywhere. Same for the TUI argv in window 0, which will show 'daemon disconnected' against the wrong socket. FakeAdapter already solves this with an explicit --home flag (fake.ts:26), proving the gap was understood for tests but not applied to the real adapters — a sharp trap the first time anyone runs a second holo instance for testing alongside the dev one (HOLO_HOME is exactly the documented mechanism for that).
confirmed.suggestion: Embed the resolved home in the injected command (e.g. HOLO_HOME='<quoted holoHome()>' prefix in hookCommand, mirroring fake-agent's --home), and pass -e HOLO_HOME=... / -e HOLO_TMUX_SESSION=... to tmux new-session/new-window for the TUI and agent windows so the whole chain pins to the daemon's actual home.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by full code trace. hookCommand() (adapters/claude.ts:35-38, shared by codex.ts:47) embeds only bun path + hook script + harness + session id — no HOLO_HOME. RealTmux.ensureSession/newWindow (tmux.ts:65-104) pass no -e env flags and nothing in tui/src calls tmux set-environment, so panes (and the hooks claude/codex spawn from them) inherit the tmux SERVER's environment, not the daemon's. The hook resolves the socket from its own env (hook/main.ts → client.ts:22 → paths.ts:10 `process.env.HOLO_HOME ?? ~/.holo`). With a custom HOLO_HOME and a pre-existing tmux server, the daemon listens on $HOLO_HOME/holod.sock while hooks dial ~/.holo/holod.sock; every hook failure path exits 0 silently by design, so the session sits stuck forever (label is 'starting…', not 'awaiting first prompt' as the finding says — minor inaccuracy, since 'ready' never arrives). The cross-daemon claim is true verbatim: server.ts:179 replies `{ ok: true }` with the comment 'always ack fast, even unknown session', silently dropping the event — and deterministic ids like 'claude-1' can even collide with the other daemon's sessions. The TUI argv (daemon/main.ts:18-23) likewise carries no home, so window 0 subscribes to the wrong socket. Tests handle this explicitly while real adapters don't: FakeAdapter passes --home (fake.ts:26) consumed by fake-agent.ts:76-77, e2e.test.ts:180 pins HOLO_HOME in child env, and smoke.test.ts only passes because its isolated `tmux -L` server is started fresh by the test process and so inherits HOLO_HOME — exactly the inheritance absent with an already-running server (the normal state when running a second instance beside the dev one). README.md:21,84 documents HOLO_HOME as the sandboxed-instance mechanism, so the trap is on a documented path, and it is not among the 8 known-intentional deviations. Caveats: fresh-tmux-server and default-home cases work fine, and the HOLO_TMUX_SESSION half is largely moot (daemon/CLI resolve it with correct env) — so 'minor' severity is honest.

confirmed.title: Wall-clock regression silently freezes a session's event acceptance for the duration of the step
confirmed.description: The stale guard (acceptEvent, line 208) compares Date.now() stamps taken in independent hook processes. The clock is same-machine but not monotonic: macOS sleep/wake NTP corrections routinely step the clock backwards by seconds. After a backward step of S seconds, every new hook event for any recently-active session carries ts < lastEventTs and is rejected for up to S seconds — prompts, stops, and notifications vanish without any log, leaving stale statuses in the queue (e.g. a session stuck 'running' that actually stopped). Hooks racing with slow connects under load have the same shape but are bounded by the 1s ack timeout; the clock step is the variant that can hit every session at once after the laptop wakes — a daily dogfooding event.
confirmed.suggestion: Tolerate bounded skew: reject only when ts < lastEventTs - SKEW_MS (e.g. 2-5s covers process-spawn races without freezing on clock steps), or clamp stored lastEventTs to Math.min(ts, now) on accept so a forward-skewed stamp can't poison the guard. Keep exact ordering only within the skew window where it actually disambiguates the designed stale-Stop case.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the full event path. (1) Hook processes stamp events with wall-clock Date.now() at emit time (src/hook/main.ts:89 for 'hook', :108 for 'permission'); each hook is an independent short-lived process. (2) The daemon forwards req.ts raw into the registry (src/daemon/server.ts:178) — its injectable now() is never used for the stale guard. (3) acceptEvent (src/daemon/registry.ts:210-216, comparison at line 212) strictly rejects ts < lastEventTs with no skew tolerance; grep confirms no clamping/skew handling anywhere. (4) Rejection is fully silent: applyEvent returns false, the server still replies {ok:true}, nothing is logged or broadcast. (5) Crucially, rejected events are dropped, not deferred — a 'stop' or 'notification' that fires inside the post-regression window is lost forever, and since a stopped/blocked session emits no further hooks on its own, the session stays 'running' in the queue indefinitely, defeating the tool's core purpose. (6) Not mitigated elsewhere: registry.test.ts stale-guard tests use a single injected logical clock and never cover regression; lastEventTs resets only on daemon restart/pruneExited; the tmux sweep only catches closed windows. (7) Not in the known-intentional deviations list. So after a backward wall-clock step (macOS timed steps the clock, e.g. post sleep/wake), any session whose lastEventTs was stamped pre-step rejects all events until the clock catches up — the claimed scenario is real. Honest caveats: the finding slightly overstates frequency ('routinely'/'daily dogfooding event') since the step must land while sessions are actively emitting (stamps pre-correction, new events post-correction within S seconds), but with parallel agents emitting 'tool' events every few seconds this is realistically reachable; 'minor' severity is honest. Trivial nit: acceptEvent is at line 210-212, not 208. The suggested fix (bounded skew window or clamping to min(ts, now)) is sound — the designed stale-Stop ordering case only needs discrimination within sub-second races, which a 2-5s skew window preserves.

confirmed.title: NewSessionModal enter key has no in-flight guard — double-press spawns duplicate sessions
confirmed.description: submit() (line 81) fires onSubmit and only reacts to the result asynchronously; nothing disables further submits while the daemon's 'new' request is in flight. The spawn path is slow enough to race (tmux ensureSession + adapter settings write + new-window can take hundreds of ms), and the modal stays open until the response arrives, so a double-tapped enter — likely for the stated ADHD-optimized '~3 keystrokes' fast path — spawns two tmux windows and two sessions. The second spawn also steals focus via jump-on-spawn, and the user must notice and manually kill the duplicate agent window.
confirmed.suggestion: Track a submitting flag (set before onSubmit, cleared on failure) in the modal's live ref and ignore enter/digit submissions while it's set; optionally render 'spawning…' in place of the key hints. Same guard applies to App.handleSpawn if other key paths can reach it.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by tracing the full path. (1) NewSessionModal.tsx submit() (line 81-88) has no in-flight guard — it only checks harness!==null and cwd!=='', fires void onSubmit().then(), and changes no state that would block re-entry; the step-2 enter handler (line 131) reaches it on every press via the live ref. (2) The modal stays mounted and keyboard-armed for the whole round trip: App.handleSpawn (App.tsx:169-180) awaits gateway.request({cmd:'new'}) and calls setModalOpen(false) only after the ok response, while App's own key handler defers to the modal whenever modalOpen (App.tsx:121). (3) Nothing downstream dedupes: client.request() (client.ts:16-40) opens a fresh unix socket per call, and the daemon's handleNew (server.ts:253-296) unconditionally createSession + tmux.newWindow + selectWindow per request — two requests deterministically produce two sessions/windows, and server.ts:282 confirms the second spawn steals focus via jump-on-spawn. (4) The race window is concrete: the spawn path runs 4-5 subprocesses (adapter.configured probe, tmux has-session, installReturnBinding, new-window, select-window via execFile) plus a settings-file write in the claude adapter (claude.ts:82-97), plausibly 50-200ms+, well within human double-tap timing. (5) Not covered by tests (NewSessionModal.test.tsx has no double-submit case; its ok:false test even notes the promise resolves a tick later, corroborating the gap), not in the known-intentional deviations list, and 'minor' severity is honest — the consequence is a duplicate idle agent window plus focus steal that the user must manually clean up.
